# Exact failures of quantitative concavity of the projected depth

For a mixed-integer probability measure write

    g(z)=max_x depth(z,x).

Every example below is induced by a full-dimensional convex body and has
full-dimensional continuous fibers. The examples do not refute OC.

## 1. No increasing transformation yields concavity on the real projection

Take n=d=1 and C=[-1,1] x [-1,1]. There are three integer fibers,
at z=-1,0,1, each of length two; total mass is six. Reflection in the
continuous coordinate preserves the measure. Since depth superlevel
sets are convex, averaging (z,x) and (z,-x) shows

    g(z)=depth(z,0).

The complete mixed set is centrally symmetric about (0,0), so every
closed halfspace through that point has at least half the mass. The
horizontal halfspace x>=0 has exactly half, hence g(0)=1/2.

At (-1/2,0), the two fibers indexed -1 and 0 form a centrally symmetric
subset around that point, of mass four. Any containing halfspace
captures at least two units from it, proving g(-1/2)>=1/3. The vertical
halfspace z<=-1/2 contains just one whole fiber, proving equality.

Convexity of the depth region at level 1/3 now gives
depth(-1/4,0)>=1/3. Its vertical containing halfspace z<=-1/4 again
has mass exactly two. Thus

    g(-1/2)=1/3,  g(-1/4)=1/3,  g(0)=1/2.                    (1)

For every strictly increasing real function phi on [1/3,1/2], concavity
of phi composed with g would require

    phi(1/3)>= [phi(1/3)+phi(1/2)]/2,

which is impossible. Therefore even a negative-power or logarithmic
reparametrization cannot make g concave on the full real projection.
The issue persists with positive fiber volume: purely integer normals
carry the atomic boundary mass that permits the jump at z=0.

## 2. Log-concavity already fails at integer midpoints

Let n=2,d=1 and

    P=conv{(-3,1),(2,-1),(3,0),(2,3)}, C=P x [-1,1].

The inequalities of P are

    2z_1+5z_2>=-1, z_2>=z_1-3,
    3z_1+z_2<=9, 5z_2-2z_1<=11.

Its fifteen lattice points are

    (-3,1),(-2,1),(-1,1),
    (0,0),(0,1),(0,2),
    (1,0),(1,1),(1,2),
    (2,-1),(2,0),(2,1),(2,2),(2,3),(3,0).

Direct substitution into the inequalities, or taking the allowed
integer z_2 ranges for z_1=-3,...,3, verifies this list. Every fiber
has length two, so total mass is thirty. As before, continuous
reflection and convexity of depth regions give g(z)=depth(z,0).

We will prove the exact values

    g((-2,1))=3/30,
    g((-1,1))=5/30,
    g((0,1))=9/30.                                         (2)

### A small exact cap lemma

Let A be any set of k>=2 fiber indices whose arithmetic mean is z.
For the equal intervals [-1,1] on those indices, every halfspace through
(z,0) captures at least two units of their total fiber length.

If its continuous normal component is zero, some source index has a
nonnegative normal product relative to the mean z, so a full interval
of length two belongs to the cap. Otherwise reflect the continuous
coordinate if necessary and scale that component to one. The source
cap lengths then have the form clamp(1-r_j,0,2), where sum_j r_j=0.
Put b_j=1-r_j, so sum_j b_j=k. If any b_j>=2, its capped value alone
supplies two. Otherwise clipping the negative b_j upward only increases
their sum, which is k>=2. This proves the lemma for every orientation.

### Lower certificates for (2)

At z=(-2,1), use its own half-interval (length at least one), and the
disjoint symmetric pair {(-3,1),(-1,1)}. The pair lemma supplies two
more units, for a total of three.

At z=(-1,1), use its own half-interval and the two disjoint symmetric
pairs {(-3,1),(1,1)} and {(-2,1),(0,1)}. The total is at least five.

At z=(0,1), use its own half-interval, the three disjoint symmetric pairs

    {(-2,1),(2,1)}, {(-1,1),(1,1)}, {(0,0),(0,2)},

and the disjoint triple

    {(-3,1),(1,0),(2,2)}.

The triple also has arithmetic mean (0,1). The lemma gives two units
from each pair and from the triple, in addition to one from the central
fiber, totaling nine. Every source used in these groups is distinct.

### Matching upper certificates for (2)

Write x for the one continuous coordinate. At (-2,1,0), use

    H={x>=z_1+2}.

It captures two units from the fiber (-3,1), one from (-2,1), and zero
from all others. At (-1,1,0), use H={x>=z_1+1}; this captures two units
from each of (-3,1),(-2,1), one from (-1,1), and zero from the others.

At (0,1,0), use

    H={x>=2z_1+z_2-1}.

It captures the four full fibers (-3,1),(-2,1),(-1,1),(0,0), one unit
from (0,1), and zero from the others. Fibers whose threshold is exactly
one contribute only a continuous endpoint of length zero. These are
all closed ambient halfspaces, and they prove the upper bounds.

Finally (-1,1) is the integer midpoint of (-2,1) and (0,1), but

    g((-1,1))^2=25/900<27/900
                         =g((-2,1))g((0,1)).

So g is not log-concave even when sampled only on integer points.
Every positive-power concavity inequality is stronger than the
corresponding geometric-mean inequality, and therefore fails here
as well. No assertion about every possible negative-power inequality
on the discrete sample is made by this second example.
